title: How to use one phone number on two phones
summary: Find out how to use one phone number on two phones. Learn the three ways to achieve this and why call forwarding does not carry your text messages.
body_markdown:
We may have cut the physical cord to our phones, but in many ways, we’re still “tethered.” Most people associate one phone line with one device, even if they’d like to answer calls from a variety of devices.


There are *so many* reasons for this: avoiding missed calls, working on the go, allowing multiple people to respond to a single line, or traveling abroad.


The good news? You *can* have two phones with the same number, allowing a single line to ring on multiple devices. In this article, we cover a few different ways to set this up and the benefits of having one number ring on multiple phones.


These three methods include:


1. **Carrier multi-line plans** that let you use one number on multiple devices, like T-Mobile DIGITS.
2. **Business phone plans** that allow teams to share the same phone number.
3. **Call forwarding** from one phone to another.


Keep reading to learn about each method and which one best suits your needs.


##


3 Methods to use one phone number on two phones


If you need to answer your phone number on multiple devices, you can choose from several options.


### Method 1: Using your provider’s multi-phone line plan


Depending on your phone carrier, you might have the option to use your mobile number across multiple devices. For example,[T-Mobile’s DIGITS service](https://www.t-mobile.com/business/solutions/digits) is installed as an app on compatible devices connected to WiFi. It lets you have multiple lines on several devices through the app.


However, there are a couple of shortcomings to keep in mind:


- **Limited to five devices.** Using DIGITS is straightforward, but you can only share your number with up to five devices.
- **Limited team collaboration features.** While you could have a phone line ring to multiple people on your team, they can’t easily see who has answered calls or work with shared contact information.
- **Isn’t reliable.** Multiple DIGITS users complain about how much of a hassle it is to use: see this[recent Reddit review](https://www.reddit.com/r/tmobile/comments/1sry560/digits_any_reason_to_keep_this_pos/) and this other[Reddit user review](https://www.reddit.com/r/tmobile/comments/1efbslr/anybody_still_using_the_digits_app_to_manage_a/) . If you want to use the same number on multiple devices without having login or call quality issues, you should look at a virtual phone app.

### Method 3: Using call forwarding


You can also use[call forwarding](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-forward-calls/) to send calls from one device to another. For example, you may not want to use a[personal phone number for work](https://www.quo.com/blog/using-personal-phone-for-work/) , so you have two phone numbers and two devices. Call forwarding works by routing calls from your business device to your personal device or vice versa.


Call forwarding setup depends on the device.


- On an Apple **iPhone** , you need to go into Settings and **Phone** and then select **Call forwarding** . You’ll then enter the number you want to forward your calls to.
- On an **Android** , you need to go into Settings and **Supplementary services** and then select **Call forwarding** . Android phones offer a few different forwarding options, such as forwarding all calls or only forwarding when busy or unanswered.


Call forwarding may meet your needs if you’re trying to send all calls from one device to another rather than actively using the same number on multiple devices. Here are a few additional key points to remember about call forwarding:


- **You can’t forward text messages.** While you can route calls from multiple phones to a single destination, you can’t do the same with text messages. If a customer texts instead of calling, the person holding your second phone won’t see it.
- **You can’t distinguish between personal and work calls.** When a forwarded call rings on the second device, it displays the number of the person calling you. That’s what you want, but it means you can’t easily separate your work and personal calls.


With a VoIP phone number, you can solve both of these challenges. You and your team have access to incoming calls and texts with a shared phone number. And when you receive a call, you can see whether it’s a business or personal contact .


You can read more about call forwarding setup on different carriers in our guide to[conditional call forwarding](https://www.quo.com/blog/conditional-call-forwarding/) .


##


Benefits of having one number on multiple phones


Having one number on multiple phones helps your team manage call volume as you grow. Here’s how:


- **Reduce missed calls.** With a shared number, you can set up[simultaneous ring](https://www.quo.com/product/call-routing/simultaneous-ring) so every team member receives your incoming calls. Available team members can answer the phone in real time, which cuts down on missed calls.
- **Increase first reply rate.** Since everyone on your team has access to a shared inbox, your team members can see incoming messages as they come in.
- **Share your conversation history across multiple devices.** One risk of having a phone number on a single device is that your conversation history remains stored in only one place. Even if you have a cloud backup of your chats, only you can access them. Having a number on multiple devices shares your conversations with your team, ensuring business continuity and coverage for every customer.

##


**FAQs**


**How much does it cost to have one phone number on two phones?**


Quo allows you to share one phone number across multiple devices at no additional cost. If you’re using a traditional carrier, the cost can vary: T-Mobile offers free multi-line calling with its phone plans.


**Can I get two SIM cards with the same phone number?**


No, you can’t get two SIM cards with the same phone number. Carriers issue one physical SIM card or an eSIM tied to one number. VoIP providers use virtual numbers that aren’t tied to a specific device, which is how teams can share a single phone number across multiple devices.


**How do I port my existing phone number to a VoIP service?**


Yes! It’s very easy to[port an existing number](https://www.quo.com/blog/whats-phone-number-porting/) over to Quo. Please[fill out a short porting form](https://support.quo.com/getting-started/porting/overview) in your Quo account with your previous carrier information and complete[carrier registration](https://support.quo.com/getting-started/carrier-registration/carrier-registration#carrier-registration-a2p-10dlc) . We’ll handle the rest.


**Can two cell phones receive the same incoming call?**


Yes, if you are using a VoIP phone system like Quo, you can install the app on multiple cell phones. Both phones would receive the same incoming call and ring simultaneously.


**What are the alternatives to using VoIP for business?**


The main alternatives to VoIP are traditional landlines, cellular plans, and on-premise PBX systems. Each comes with higher costs and less flexibility than a modern VoIP solution. For a full breakdown, check out our guide:[VoIP alternatives for business](https://www.quo.com/blog/voip-alternatives) .


**Is it secure to use one phone number on multiple devices?**


Every device on a shared phone number is a potential access point for hackers. As long as you’re using a reputable VoIP provider, sharing a number across devices is safe. For example,[Quo encrypts your calls](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/security-and-compliance) , text messages, and business data with AES-256 encryption and holds SOC 2 Type II certification. Just make sure any device with access is secured with a strong password or biometric lock.


**Does call forwarding show my original phone number?**


Usually, no. When a forwarded call rings on the second device, it typically displays the number of the person calling you, not your own number. This can vary by carrier and forwarding type, so if you need to reliably tell forwarded business calls apart from personal ones, a shared VoIP number is more consistent.
